learningObjective: Distinguish dominance and post-dominance relations and identify implications for SSA construction and code motion.

canonicalClaims.claim: D dominates N iff every path from the entry to N passes through D; P post-dominates N iff every path from N to the exit passes through P. Dominance forms a tree rooted at entry; post-dominance forms a tree rooted at exit and is the dual over the reverse CFG.
conditions: CFG has a distinguished entry; post-dominance requires a distinguished exit (may be synthesized for functions with multiple returns).
nonImplications: Does not imply dominance equals post-dominance except in trivial CFGs.
Does not imply the dominator tree includes unreachable code.

misconceptions.claim: Dominance and post-dominance are equivalent for any CFG.
misconceptions.whyWrong: They are duals on reverse CFG; they generally differ except in trivial linear CFGs.

misconceptions.claim: Post-dominance does not require a distinguished exit; it works for arbitrary CFGs.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Post-dominance is defined with respect to an exit; if the function has multiple returns, a synthesized virtual exit is added.

misconceptions.claim: The dominator tree includes unreachable code.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Unreachable code has no path from entry; it is outside the reachable CFG and outside the dominator tree.

implementationFacts: Lengauer-Tarjan dominator algorithm runs in nearly linear time.
Dominance frontier is used in Cytron et al. SSA construction algorithm.
Control dependence is computed from post-dominance: block B is control-dependent on block A if A has successors, one of which post-dominates B and one does not.
performanceScenarios: LICM uses dominance to prove a loop-invariant expression can be safely hoisted; post-dominance is used to prove a value is used unconditionally.
